description: We are looking for UX designers and story tellers
summary:
Space Twin finds places on Earth whose terrain resembles a chosen spot on the Moon. You pick one of 18 lunar sites, from Apollo landing zones to the south pole, on a 3D Moon, and the app compares it with 5,009 ten-kilometer patches from 73 Earth regions.

Both bodies are described by the same 12 measures of slope and relief, from NASA's LRO laser altimeter for the Moon and NASADEM (plus Copernicus in a few regions) for Earth. We add the day-night temperature swing and how often the Sun clears the local horizon. Each dimension gets its own score, so a result can read "strong terrain match, weak thermal match" instead of one vague number. That is exactly what the challenge asks for.

Our favorite part is a second chart that sets the best matches against practical questions: road access, medical help, power grid and protected land. A perfect analog inside a nature reserve won't help a team that needs to test a rover next spring. You can also ask an AI assistant about the results.

We don't pick landing sites. We shortlist the Earth places worth testing in first.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Twin starts from a spot on the Moon and looks for places on Earth that feel the same underfoot. We cut a 10 by 10 km patch around each of 18 lunar sites and around 5,009 candidate patches in 73 hand-picked Earth regions. Then we run both through the same function, which extracts 12 numbers describing slope and terrain shape. A smaller distance between two patches means more similar terrain.

Terrain comes first, but we also compare the day-night temperature swing (MODIS on Earth, LRO Diviner on the Moon) and how much of the time the Sun clears the local horizon. We computed the second one ourselves by tracing horizons over the elevation data with real Sun positions, and checked it against NASA's own LOLA visibility map at the lunar south pole, where the two agree closely (rank correlation 0.97). The ranking is 60% terrain, 20% temperature, 20% sunlight. Rock type is shown next to it but not ranked on, because the Moon side comes from orbital spectra and the Earth side is only estimated from geologic maps.

Separately, we score practicality: road access, buildable ground, medical help, power, and flags for protected areas, hazards and land rights. It never touches the ranking. A chart plots the 20 best matches by similarity against practicality and marks the trade-offs: sites where no other candidate is both closer and easier to work at. A built-in assistant answers questions using only the data for the selected site.

Benefits and intended impact

You can see which dimensions match and where the analogy breaks. Missing data is shown as missing, never counted as zero, and the tool never claims to pick a landing site. We hope it gives mission planners, students and curious people a faster way to shortlist where to rehearse lunar operations on Earth, for example which desert or lava field is worth visiting before a rover goes anywhere near the Moon.

Tools and data

Python 3.12 (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, rasterio) for the science, FastAPI for the API, and React, TypeScript, Vite and three.js for the interface. The assistant runs on Google Gemini. Data comes from NASADEM and Copernicus DEM (via Microsoft Planetary Computer), LRO LOLA and Diviner, MODIS, Macrostrat, WorldPop, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap, Malaria Atlas Project travel times, OurAirports, protected-area and volcano databases, and NASA SVS Moon maps. No special hardware is needed. The committed data runs the whole app on a laptop, and only the AI chat needs a Gemini key.

What is creative about it

We refused to give one "Moon-likeness" score. Practicality is kept apart from similarity, so a scientifically perfect but unreachable site stays visible for you to judge. The Moon itself is the interface: you spin it, pick a site, and Earth swings into view beside it with the five closest matches pinned. Both terrains then open side by side in 3D on one shared height scale, with linked cameras, so turning one turns both.

What we considered

The Moon elevation map is largely interpolated, so its slopes come out slightly smoother than Earth's. NASADEM includes treetops, which is why we chose deserts and lava fields. The Earth temperature swing is a lower bound and comes from a different instrument than the Moon's, so we compare percentiles within each body. Practicality rests on coarse data, and land rights are always marked for manual review. Gravity, vacuum and radiation are not covered, and Mars is future work.
